overviewSummary.sv: The VS Code debug configuration no longer starts `service/main.py` on the developer's own Python. Pressing F5 now builds and starts the service in a Docker container, and VS Code attaches to debugpy inside it. A new task runs `docker compose up -d --build service`. A new Dockerfile builds an image with Python 3.12, debugpy and the `service` code. A new compose.yaml starts the service under debugpy on port 5678 and publishes the service's HTTP port 8080.

overview.sv:
The VS Code debug configuration no longer starts `service/main.py` on the developer's own Python. Pressing F5 now builds and starts the service in a Docker container, and VS Code attaches to debugpy inside it. A new task runs `docker compose up -d --build service`. A new Dockerfile builds an image with Python 3.12, debugpy and the `service` code. A new compose.yaml starts the service under debugpy on port 5678 and publishes the service's HTTP port 8080.

The Python code (`service/main.py`, `service/server.py`) is the same in both revisions. Only how the service is started and debugged changes. The old local-run configuration is replaced, not kept alongside the new one, so from VS Code the service is now only debugged in the container.

title.sv: What happens when the developer presses F5
title.en: What happens when the developer presses F5

purpose.sv: Follow the chain from the launch configuration through the task, the image and the container command to the attach.
purpose.en: Follow the chain from the launch configuration through the task, the image and the container command to the attach.

question.sv: How does one debug start go from VS Code to a debugger attached to the service in a container?
question.en: How does one debug start go from VS Code to a debugger attached to the service in a container?

title.sv: Before: the service ran on the local Python
title.en: Before: the service ran on the local Python

summary.sv: The old configuration launched `service/main.py` directly in VS Code's terminal.
summary.en: The old configuration launched `service/main.py` directly in VS Code's terminal.

body.sv:
In the base revision, F5 started `service/main.py` with `"request": "launch"`. That means debugpy started the program itself, on whatever Python the developer had selected, in the integrated terminal. No container was involved, and the debugger was there from the first line.

The next steps show what replaces this. The program is now started somewhere else, and VS Code only connects to it.
body.en:
In the base revision, F5 started `service/main.py` with `"request": "launch"`. That means debugpy started the program itself, on whatever Python the developer had selected, in the integrated terminal. No container was involved, and the debugger was there from the first line.

The next steps show what replaces this. The program is now started somewhere else, and VS Code only connects to it.

why.sv: This way of running the service is removed from the workspace. Anyone who relied on F5 to debug without Docker loses that option.
why.en: This way of running the service is removed from the workspace. Anyone who relied on F5 to debug without Docker loses that option.

title.sv: The configuration now attaches, after a task
title.en: The configuration now attaches, after a task

summary.sv: `request: attach` plus `preLaunchTask` means: first run a task, then connect to a debugger that is already running.
summary.en: `request: attach` plus `preLaunchTask` means: first run a task, then connect to a debugger that is already running.

body.sv:
With `"request": "attach"`, VS Code no longer starts any process. It expects a debugpy server to be listening at `connect` (`localhost:5678`) and connects to it.

What gets that server running is `preLaunchTask`. VS Code runs the task with this label, shown in the next step, and starts the attach only once the task has finished. **The whole start-up of the service has moved into that task.**
body.en:
With `"request": "attach"`, VS Code no longer starts any process. It expects a debugpy server to be listening at `connect` (`localhost:5678`) and connects to it.

What gets that server running is `preLaunchTask`. VS Code runs the task with this label, shown in the next step, and starts the attach only once the task has finished. **The whole start-up of the service has moved into that task.**

details.sv: `pathMappings` and `justMyCode` belong to the same configuration. They decide how breakpoints and stepping work once attached, which the second walk covers.
details.en: `pathMappings` and `justMyCode` belong to the same configuration. They decide how breakpoints and stepping work once attached, which the second walk covers.

title.sv: The task builds and starts the container
title.en: The task builds and starts the container

summary.sv: A shell task runs `docker compose up -d --build service`.
summary.en: A shell task runs `docker compose up -d --build service`.

body.sv:
This task is reached through its `label`, which matches the `preLaunchTask` in the previous step.

- `--build` rebuilds the image on every debug start. This is how local code changes get into the container, because the code is copied into the image (Dockerfile step) and not mounted.
- `-d` runs the container in the background, so the command returns once Compose has started it. That is when VS Code goes on to attach.

The container's start is not the same as debugpy listening. Nothing in the task waits until port 5678 accepts connections. Whether the first attach succeeds therefore depends on how fast debugpy starts inside the container. The configuration does not guarantee it.

why.sv: Stopping the debugger only disconnects. The container started with `-d` keeps running until someone stops it with Docker.
why.en: Stopping the debugger only disconnects. The container started with `-d` keeps running until someone stops it with Docker.

details.sv: The task has no `problemMatcher`. VS Code may then ask whether to continue without scanning the task output. That only affects the prompt, not what runs.
details.en: The task has no `problemMatcher`. VS Code may then ask whether to continue without scanning the task output. That only affects the prompt, not what runs.

title.sv: The image: Python, debugpy and a copy of the code
title.en: The image: Python, debugpy and a copy of the code

body.sv:
Compose builds this image because of `build: .` for the `service` service. The image adds two things to `python:3.12-slim`:

- debugpy is installed, so the container command can run under it.
- The local `service` folder is copied to `/app/service`, with `/app` as the working directory.

Because `/app` is the working directory and the code sits in `/app/service`, `service` can be imported as a package. That is what the `-m service.main` command in the next step and the `from service.server import serve` in `main.py` need.
body.en:
Compose builds this image because of `build: .` for the `service` service. The image adds two things to `python:3.12-slim`:

- debugpy is installed, so the container command can run under it.
- The local `service` folder is copied to `/app/service`, with `/app` as the working directory.

Because `/app` is the working directory and the code sits in `/app/service`, `service` can be imported as a package. That is what the `-m service.main` command in the next step and the `from service.server import serve` in `main.py` need.

why.sv: The container runs a snapshot of the code taken at build time. Its Python version is set by the image, no longer by the developer's interpreter.
why.en: The container runs a snapshot of the code taken at build time. Its Python version is set by the image, no longer by the developer's interpreter.

title.sv: The container runs the service under debugpy
title.en: The container runs the service under debugpy

summary.sv: debugpy listens on 5678 and runs `service.main`; both 5678 and 8080 are published.
summary.en: debugpy listens on 5678 and runs `service.main`; both 5678 and 8080 are published.

body.sv:
This command is what the container runs once the task from earlier has started it. `python -m debugpy --listen 0.0.0.0:5678 -m service.main` opens debugpy's server on all of the container's interfaces and runs `service.main` as a module.

There is **no `--wait-for-client`**. The service starts straight away, without waiting for VS Code. Code that runs before the attach does not stop at breakpoints. For this service that is just the call into `serve`, before it starts serving.

The `ports` entries publish 5678, so VS Code can reach it at `localhost:5678`, and 8080, where the HTTP server listens.

There is **no `--wait-for-client`**. The service starts straight away, without waiting for VS Code. Code that runs before the attach does not stop at breakpoints. For this service that is just the call into `serve`, before it starts serving.

The `ports` entries publish 5678, so VS Code can reach it at `localhost:5678`, and 8080, where the HTTP server listens.

why.sv: A port written as `"5678:5678"` is published on all of the host's interfaces, not only localhost. A debugpy port lets whoever connects run code in the process.
why.en: A port written as `"5678:5678"` is published on all of the host's interfaces, not only localhost. A debugpy port lets whoever connects run code in the process.

title.sv: What runs inside: the unchanged service
title.en: What runs inside: the unchanged service

summary.sv: `main` calls `serve(port=8080)`, which serves HTTP forever on 0.0.0.0.
summary.en: `main` calls `serve(port=8080)`, which serves HTTP forever on 0.0.0.0.

body.sv:
This is the module the debugpy command from the previous step runs. It is unchanged. It is shown because two of the new settings depend on it:

- It binds to `0.0.0.0`, which is needed for the published port 8080 to reach it from outside the container.
- `serve_forever` keeps the process alive, so the container keeps running and debugpy stays available to attach to.

title.sv: How a breakpoint in the local file reaches the container
title.en: How a breakpoint in the local file reaches the container

purpose.sv: Understand path mapping, why the code must be rebuilt, and what `justMyCode: false` changes.
purpose.en: Understand path mapping, why the code must be rebuilt, and what `justMyCode: false` changes.

question.sv: Why does a breakpoint set in the editor stop the code running at /app/service?
question.en: Why does a breakpoint set in the editor stop the code running at /app/service?

title.sv: Local and container paths are mapped
title.en: Local and container paths are mapped

body.sv:
The editor knows the file as `<workspace>/service/server.py`. The process in the container runs it as `/app/service/server.py`, because the Dockerfile copies the code there. `pathMappings` tells debugpy how to translate between the two. Without it, breakpoints would not bind, and stack frames would not open the local file.

The mapping only matches if the copy in the image is the same as the local file. That holds because the start task builds with `--build` on each F5. If the developer edits a file while attached and does not restart, the lines in the editor and in the container can drift apart.

label.sv: Where the code lands in the image
label.en: Where the code lands in the image

summary.sv: `justMyCode: false` lets the debugger stop in and step into code outside the project.
summary.en: `justMyCode: false` lets the debugger stop in and step into code outside the project.

body.sv:
With `justMyCode` off, the debugger also stops in, and steps into, the standard library and installed packages. For this service that mostly means `http.server`, which does the real request handling.

Those library files live in the container's Python installation, which `pathMappings` does not cover. VS Code then cannot open them as local files. It has to show the source it gets from the debugger instead, which may be read-only or not match the local Python.
